channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Aviation
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Manchester Airports Group data published in full after the ransom was refused — airport operations untouched
item.category: Top Story
item.description: Manchester Airports Group refused to pay, and on 3 September the group calling itself FulcrumSec published what it says is the full haul: roughly 550GB taken from MAG’s customer systems. HaveIBeenPwned parsed about 8.8 million email addresses from the dump, alongside phone numbers, postcodes and vehicle registrations drawn from car park, lounge and Fast Track bookings and in-airport Wi-Fi sign-ups at Manchester, London Stansted and East Midlands. MAG, which disclosed the breach on 27 August, says the records sat in a database hosted by a third party, that no payment details were taken, and that airport operations were not affected. FulcrumSec’s claim that it found administrative keys exposed in front-end JavaScript has not been independently verified. For airport operators the material question is custody: who holds passenger data, on whose infrastructure, and how far that estate sits from anything operational. - SecurityWeek reporting on Manchester Airports Group statements, with the record count taken from HaveIBeenPwned’s parsing of the published data - Breach disclosed by MAG 27 Aug 2026; stolen data published by FulcrumSec 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [Not Cyber] UK flight-data processing failed and more than 2,000 flights went with it — NATS ruled out a cyberattack, and the regulator is now reviewing the resilience that broke
item.category: Context — ATC operational failure; a cyberattack was explicitly ruled out by the operator
item.description: This is not a cyber incident. It is carried here, clearly labelled, because it is the aviation infrastructure story of the period and readers will reasonably have wondered. On 8 September a fault in the flight-data processing chain at NATS, the UK air navigation service provider, forced Heathrow to suspend arrivals and disrupted Gatwick and Manchester, affecting more than 2,000 flights across 8–9 September with over a thousand cancellations reported on the first day. NATS chief executive Martin Rolfe told BBC Radio that “we have at this point ruled out cyber”; no threat actor has claimed the event, no agency has opened a cyber investigation, and nothing in the reporting points to an intrusion. NATS’ own timeline puts fault identification at 15:25, a fix implemented by 16:40 and normal operations restored by 19:30 the same day — a four-hour technical event that took two days to clear from the schedule. The reported root cause, that a flight plan filed for a UK military aircraft introduced anomalous data the processing system could not handle, is contested: the account was disputed and the Ministry of Defence has pushed back on a military-error framing, so treat the cause as unresolved pending the NATS investigation and the review. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said she did not accept that the failure was “unavoidable” and has ordered an independent Civil Aviation Authority review of NATS resilience, due within six months. For aviation OT teams the value is availability engineering rather than attack defence, with one security lesson attached: a system that cannot safely reject anomalous input from a trusted upstream feed has a security problem sitting behind its reliability one, because malformed data is exactly what an attacker sends when direct access is unavailable. - AeroTime reporting on the NATS timeline and the contested military flight-plan account, with AP on the cancellation totals and NATS chief executive Martin Rolfe’s BBC Radio remarks ruling out cyber - Failure 8 Sep 2026; cyber publicly ruled out 10 Sep 2026; independent CAA resilience review ordered, follow-up reporting verified 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Three airports stopped flying for drones inside ten days, and one of them for a flock of birds — the gap is detection, not defence
item.category: Incident — Airspace intrusion and detection; no cyber component
item.description: Brussels Airport halted traffic for roughly half an hour on the evening of Friday 12 September after a drone was sighted near the airfield; no injuries or damage were reported and movements resumed once the area was cleared, with the drone’s origin and intent unattributed. The following day Vilnius closed for 38 minutes on a drone alert that scrambled a NATO jet before the object was confirmed to be a flock of birds. Both follow the US Labor Day weekend incursion at San Diego that grounded around 400 flights, where the TSA reportedly could not identify the operator and coverage noted that US airports carry no mandatory drone-detection requirement at all. None of this is a cyberattack and none of it should be filed as one. It belongs on this page because the operational consequence is identical to an OT failure and lands on the same people: a ground stop cascades into stand and gate reallocation, jet-bridge and ramp re-sequencing, baggage re-flow and fuel and de-icing re-planning, and the decision to stop or resume is increasingly taken from software — counter-UAS detection feeds, ground-movement displays, airfield lighting control — that few airports treat as operational technology with an integrity requirement. Vilnius is the instructive one: the cost was not the drone, it was the ambiguity. - Reuters reporting on the Brussels Airport halt, with IJR on the Vilnius closure and NATO scramble and Tech Times on the San Diego grounding and the absence of a US detection mandate - Brussels 12 Sep 2026; Vilnius 13 Sep 2026; San Diego over the Labor Day weekend, 4–7 Sep 2026, carried as preceding context

item.title: [High] A China-linked crew is emptying self-hosted code repositories of SCADA and HMI source — and aerospace is on the victim list
item.category: Incident — State-linked source-code and credential theft from self-hosted developer infrastructure
item.description: Acronis threat intelligence, reported on 14–15 September, describes a campaign it attributes with moderate confidence to a China-linked actor it calls Red Heron, exploiting a critical remote code execution flaw in the self-hosted Gitea code platform, CVE-2026-60004, since 29 July. The actor scanned 1,386 internet-facing Gitea instances across seven countries and confirmed compromises at 13 organisations in six, the victim set spanning aerospace, telecommunications, government, elections and defence alongside industry. Two victims define the objective: a Taiwanese industrial-automation company whose stolen repositories covered SCADA and HMI tooling, IoT platform integrations and network-sniffer products, and a Canadian renewable-energy firm from which infrastructure maps, configuration secrets, SSH host keys and internal tokens were taken. The implant, a custom loader Acronis calls JITTERLY with an embedded Linux rootkit named SIXZUT, supports more than thirty post-exploitation commands. Nothing here is aviation-specific and no airport or airline has been named, but the pattern is the one that reaches this sector indirectly: MRO software houses, baggage and BMS integrators and ground-systems developers routinely keep deployment configurations, VPN profiles, device credentials and site diagrams in self-hosted repositories that sit outside anyone’s OT security programme. Stolen host keys and infrastructure maps are not the attack; they are the preparation for one that arrives later looking like legitimate maintenance access. - Industrial Cyber and The Hacker News reporting on Acronis threat-intelligence research into the Red Heron campaign - Exploitation traced to 29 Jul 2026; campaign reporting published 14–15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] FBI seizes the Chinese state-sponsored platforms that scanned critical infrastructure and relayed attacks through hijacked devices
item.category: Incident — Law-enforcement seizure of state-sponsored attack infrastructure
item.description: The Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures on 26 August of QScan and QTRouter, two linked platforms run by a PRC state-sponsored group the government calls QTFY and ties to a Nanjing contractor. QScan handled reconnaissance against US critical infrastructure; QTRouter relayed the resulting intrusions through compromised routers and IoT devices so traffic arrived from ordinary domestic addresses. Both are now inoperable because the seized domains were hard-coded into the malware. Named victims are federal, including NASA, and the described activity runs back to at least 2018. For airports and airlines the relay layer is the transferable lesson: a terminal building is dense with small, internet-connected, unowned devices, and source addresses in your logs never proved anything. - US Department of Justice press release and unsealed court documents — corroborated by TechCrunch and UPI - Seizures announced and confirmed 26 Aug 2026; described activity dates from at least 2018 to 2026

item.title: [High] Norway spent forty minutes convincing a rescue helicopter it was somewhere else — and the avionics never reported a fault
item.category: Research — GNSS spoofing against airborne receivers; controlled exercise, not an attack
item.description: At Jammertest 2026, the annual open interference exercise on Andøya, researchers escalated a spoofing signal on 10 September until a rescue helicopter’s GPS display showed a false position out over the Norwegian Sea and a track of tight overlapping turns, while the aircraft in fact flew normally. The finding worth carrying is the detection asymmetry rather than the spectacle: jamming announces itself as signal loss and crews are trained for it, whereas spoofing leaves the receiver confidently reporting data that is internally consistent, plausible and wrong. This was a controlled test, not an in-the-wild incident, and no aircraft was endangered. It lands against a real backdrop the researchers cited — RAF aircraft encountering GPS jamming near the Russian border and daily GNSS interference over Sweden through 2026 — and it reinforces the updated jamming and spoofing guidance EASA issued to operators in July 2026. For airport operators the read-across runs past the flight deck. GNSS is not only a navigation input; it is a cheap and widely deployed time source, and GNSS-disciplined clocks quietly underpin surveillance feeds, surface-movement and logging across ground estates. A time source that can be walked rather than broken is a category of failure most airport OT inventories have never recorded. - TechSpot reporting on the Jammertest 2026 exercise at Andøya, with the regulatory backdrop from EASA’s July 2026 jamming and spoofing guidance - Exercise and reporting 10 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] August set a global ransomware record at 997 attacks, with utilities among the categories driving the rise
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Sector statistics
item.description: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — an average of 32 a day, a 23 percent increase on July’s 809, and above the previous monthly record of 988. The reporting singles out utility, healthcare and business-services attacks as the categories behind the surge. Treat the absolute number with the usual caution — counts of this kind depend on leak-site claims and disclosure practice as much as on actual incident volume, and claimed victims are not confirmed victims. The direction of travel, however, is consistent with what operators are seeing. Airlines, airports and their service providers sit inside the business-services and transport categories driving this figure. Aviation's recent history is consistent: the encryption lands on a shared IT provider or a back-office system, and the visible failure is at check-in, baggage or turnaround rather than in a control system. - Comparitech monthly ransomware tracking — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Data for August 2026; reporting published 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Cyber-informed engineering argues the useful question is not how to keep attackers out, but which consequences you can design away
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Analysis, engineering practice
item.description: An analysis published 15 September sets out the case for cyber-informed engineering in critical infrastructure: that industrial systems operate under a constraint IT does not share, because a compromised network does not automatically have to become a catastrophic physical event. The argument is to move the security question upstream into design — identifying the physical consequences that actually matter, then engineering them out with controls that do not depend on the digital system remaining trustworthy. Aviation's safety culture already embeds the principle — independent systems, engineered fallbacks, defined degraded modes. The argument here is to apply it explicitly to airport and airline OT, asking where a network compromise could produce a physical or safety consequence and what design change would remove that possibility. This is practitioner analysis rather than incident reporting; it names no victim and describes no attack, but it is the most useful lens available for operators whose detection budget will never match their consequence exposure. - Industrial Cyber feature analysis on cyber-informed engineering - Published 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Google reports a financially motivated group running a full credential-harvesting campaign with autonomous agents in under six hours
item.category: Threat intelligence — Autonomous agent frameworks in live intrusion operations
item.description: Google’s Threat Intelligence Group reported on 8 September that a financially motivated actor stood up and executed a large-scale credential-harvesting campaign in less than six hours using an autonomous multi-agent framework, with the agents handling stages that previously took an operator days. GTIG also observed actors going after proprietary AI models across healthcare, government and media, stealing API credentials and hijacking victim cloud tenants to run their own workloads on someone else’s bill. Its guidance is to assume every threat actor now uses AI somewhere in the chain. For airports and airlines the exposure is the credential estate around operations: crew and ground-handler portals, ground-support scheduling, maintenance and MRO tooling, and the federated identity that increasingly sits behind vendor access to terminal and airside systems. - Google Threat Intelligence Group research reported by The Hacker News, including comment from GTIG’s John Hultquist - Published and reported 8 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Ukraine formally notifies aviation authorities that Russian airspace presents a growing risk to civil aircraft
item.category: Operational risk — Airspace safety and navigation integrity, not a cyber incident
item.description: Ukraine issued a formal notification to international aviation authorities on 2 September warning that Russian airspace carries growing risk to civil aviation, a day after President Zelenskyy urged airlines and insurers to stop using Russian airspace and airports as long-range drone operations expand. Russia’s civil aviation regulator rejected the warning. This is an airspace-safety and geopolitical matter rather than a cyber event, and most Western carriers have avoided the airspace since 2022 — but it belongs on an OT dashboard for one reason. The same operating environment has produced sustained regional GNSS jamming and spoofing, and navigation-integrity degradation is the point where an external, non-cyber disruption starts behaving like an attack on a safety system: correct equipment, wrong answers. - Euronews reporting on Ukraine’s formal notification to international aviation authorities and the response from Russia’s civil aviation regulator - Notification issued and reported 2 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Eighteen frontier models were run at a real enterprise network — one completed the whole kill chain unaided
item.category: Research — measured autonomous attack capability in frontier AI models; no incident
item.description: Booz Allen published its Cyber Weapon Index and an accompanying report on 4 September, grading eighteen frontier AI models on how much of an intrusion they can carry out without a human driving. The models were run against a representative enterprise network rather than a benchmark; the top performer completed the full sequence — reconnaissance, initial access, lateral movement and objective — unaided, while most managed individual stages. The authors’ conclusion is about time rather than novelty: nothing in the tested behaviour was a new technique, but the interval between a foothold and a consequence compresses when the attacker never pauses to think. Booz Allen also reports that defensive playbooks written specifically against autonomous attackers cut their success rate by more than 95% in the same tests. For an airport the implication is the overnight window — baggage, fuelling and BMS controls sit behind facility networks that are watched hardest during the operating day, not at 3 am. - Booz Allen Cyber Weapon Index and the report “The Offensive Frontier: AI as the Attacker”, reported by Industrial Cyber — vendor-published research; the figures are the authors’ own test results and have not been independently reproduced - Published and reported 4 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Six steps to being able to disconnect airside systems — and a three-month planning horizon
item.category: Research — Isolation readiness, practitioner guidance
item.description: Nozomi Networks published a practitioner summary on 2 September of the Five Eyes “CI Fortify” guidance released in late July, reducing it to six steps: identify vital systems and their dependencies; establish trust levels and connection maps; pre-build the separation points; create and test graduated isolation plans; retain visibility while isolated; and run post-isolation checks before reconnecting. For airports the first step is the awkward one, because so many vital systems belong to someone else — common-use check-in, baggage reconciliation, ground-handling platforms. The recent European airport disruptions showed manual fallback working for check-in but not scaling. Nozomi’s suggestion that operators plan to sustain isolated operations for up to three months is worth reading against airside plant specifically: BMS, access control and airfield lighting need to keep running whether or not the terminal IT estate does. - Nozomi Networks Labs analysis of the CISA / ASD ACSC / NCSC-UK / CCCS “CI Fortify” guidance - Analysis published 2 Sep 2026; underlying guidance published 28 Jul 2026

item.title: [Critical] NCSC issues an alert: increased targeting of OT across multiple sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
item.category: Threat Intelligence — National agency alert on OT targeting
item.description: The NCSC published a formal alert on 27 August stating it has seen increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK, by a range of threat actors, with some limited real-world disruption already resulting. It names no victims, actors or techniques, and it landed the same day Manchester Airports Group disclosed its breach — a coincidence of timing, not a link. Aviation is not called out, but the exposure the NCSC describes is the airport’s: a campus estate of controllers bought as part of a building fit-out, supported remotely by an OEM, and rarely re-surveyed. Baggage handling drives, jet bridge controllers, de-icing and fuelling telemetry, airfield lighting cabinets, stand equipment, BMS and access control all sit in that category, and the instruction not to assume they are unreachable from the internet without verifying it is the whole point of the alert. - UK National Cyber Security Centre alert, “Disruptive cyber activity highlights risk from internet-exposed systems and edge devices” - Published 27 Aug 2026; the NCSC says it has been engaging affected sectors directly ahead of publication

item.title: [Critical] GitLab CVSS 10 path traversal is being exploited, and airport and airline teams host more of it than they think
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: GitLab patched CVE-2026-85706 on 10 September, a path-traversal flaw in the repository commits API that it rated CVSS 10.0 and that allows an unauthenticated attacker to read arbitrary files from a GitLab server. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday 11 September with a remediation deadline for federal agencies of Monday 14 September. watchTowr reported it was already seeing in-the-wild probes for vulnerable servers, and Hong Kong’s CERT issued its own advisory on 14 September stating the flaw is being exploited in the wild. A second flaw fixed in the same release, CVE-2026-87719, can expose sensitive information from Enterprise Edition servers. Airport and airline estates version baggage-handling integrations, gate and stand allocation logic, BMS and access-control middleware, MRO systems and airline operations tooling in self-hosted GitLab. Unauthenticated file reads against those servers surface the service accounts and API keys that reach airside and terminal systems. - GitLab patch release advisory and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — reporting via Cybersecurity Dive - GitLab patch published 10 Sep 2026; KEV listing 11 Sep 2026; reporting 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Four PROFINET DCP flaws in the Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 edge gateway — patched, unexploited, and worth an inventory check
item.category: Advisory — Vendor patch, vulnerability research
item.description: Nozomi Networks Labs disclosed four memory-corruption vulnerabilities in the PROFINET Discovery and basic Configuration Protocol implementation on the Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 industrial PC, published 15 September. Tracked as CVE-2025-40575 through CVE-2025-40578, each carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 5.3 and affects firmware up to V4.0 HF0. The set comprises an uninitialised-value flaw, a NULL pointer dereference and two out-of-bounds reads. The flawed DCP daemon runs as root, requires no authentication and is bound to all three device interfaces, so an attacker with access to the same Layer 2 segment can crash it with crafted Ethernet frames — making the device appear unreachable to SCADA, or preventing it from obtaining an IP address during commissioning. Siemens has fixed the flaws in current firmware and published security report SSA-327438. There is no reported exploitation. Airport plant rooms, baggage systems and airfield equipment that use the LPE9403 as a PROFINET edge collector inherit this. The flawed DCP daemon runs as root and unauthenticated on all three interfaces, so anyone who reaches the same Layer 2 segment — including a contractor's laptop in a plant room — can crash it. - Nozomi Networks Labs research and Siemens ProductCERT SSA-327438 — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Research and reporting published 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Sandworm and a Qilin affiliate are exploiting Cisco firewall management — the boundary between airport IT and airfield OT
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is being exploited in the wild. The flaw is a critical authentication bypass caused by an improper system process created at boot; a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and gains root on the underlying operating system. Cisco patched it in early March and added indicators of compromise in late July, then disclosed on 9 September that it had observed exploitation from August. CISA added the CVE to its KEV catalog with a 12 September federal deadline, which has now passed. Cisco Talos reports three clusters abusing this flaw and the earlier CVE-2026-20316: one deploying a web shell and malicious JAR to harvest credentials, one attributed to the Russian state actor Sandworm delivering Cyclops Blink, and one tied to Qilin ransomware enumerating endpoints for encryption. Airports should treat this as an airfield-and-terminal segmentation problem rather than an office IT patch. The firewalls FMC configures are usually what stands between the corporate network and baggage handling, jet bridges, fuelling, de-icing, airfield lighting, BMS and access control. - Cisco security advisory update and Cisco Talos research of 9 Sep 2026, plus the CISA KEV addition of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek - Advisory updated and KEV listing added 9 Sep 2026; reporting 10 Sep 2026 — re-verified 13 Sep 2026, no change of state; KEV federal deadline of 12 Sep 2026 now passed

item.title: [Critical] ScreenConnect is being used to push scripts to endpoints as they connect — the console your handlers and integrators already have on your estate
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-84869 in ConnectWise ScreenConnect to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 12 September with a federal remediation deadline of 14 September. The flaw is a missing authorisation check rated CVSS 9.9 that permits unauthorised file transfer and code execution, and three separate incidents have been documented in which threat actors abused it to push malicious scripts to endpoints as those endpoints newly connected to a server. That detail is the one that matters operationally: the malicious action arrives through the legitimate management channel, signed off by the tool the estate is built to trust, so it looks like maintenance rather than intrusion. ScreenConnect and its peers are the standing path by which ground handlers, baggage and BMS maintainers, access-control contractors and airport systems integrators reach terminal systems out of hours, frequently on instances the airport authority neither owns nor patches. It sits alongside this week’s other confirmed remote-access exploitation as a single theme: the attacker is no longer forcing a boundary, they are borrowing the support tool that already crosses it. - CISA KEV catalog addition of 12 Sep 2026, reported by The Hacker News alongside the Artifactory and RouterOS additions in the same batch - KEV listing 12 Sep 2026; federal deadline 14 Sep 2026, now passed

item.title: [Critical] NetScaler is being probed harder than it is being patched — 56 exploitation attempts in a week against an authentication bypass now in KEV
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-19490 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 9 September, an authentication bypass rated CVSS 9.3 affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway in AAA virtual server and Gateway configurations, with a federal deadline of 12 September that has now passed. Honeypot telemetry logged 56 exploitation attempts from 3 September onward, 36 of them on 8 September alone, which is the shape of opportunistic mass scanning rather than targeted intrusion — internet-facing devices are being found and tried before their owners finish the change window. It arrived in the same KEV batch as the Fortinet FortiOS, FortiSwitchManager and FortiSASE heap overflow CVE-2025-25249, exploited since July and linked to a campaign that has infected an estimated 178 FortiGate devices with the PivotC2 remote access trojan. Aviation reads these as one exposure. NetScaler Gateway is a common front door for airline crew and operations portals, engineering and MRO applications and third-party access into terminal systems, and FortiGate is among the most common devices sitting on the boundary between an airport’s corporate network and its airside estate. An authentication bypass on either is not a data-theft problem, it is a segmentation problem. - CISA KEV additions of 9 Sep 2026 for Citrix NetScaler and Fortinet FortiOS, reported by The Hacker News with honeypot exploitation telemetry - KEV listings 9 Sep 2026; federal deadline 12 Sep 2026, now passed; Fortinet exploitation traced to Jul 2026

item.title: [Critical] MikroTik RouterOS “MikroTrick” chain moves from disclosed to confirmed exploited — CERT Polska
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploitation newly confirmed in the wild
item.description: CERT Polska issued an alert on 9 September confirming that the MikroTik RouterOS vulnerabilities known as the “MikroTrick” chain — previously disclosed but not confirmed exploited — are now being used in real-world attacks, with activity observed since at least 2 September. The chain pairs an SSH authentication-bypass flaw, CVE-2026-67276 at CVSS 9.2, with an SSH privilege-escalation flaw, CVE-2026-86060 also at CVSS 9.2, to take full unauthenticated administrative control of an internet-exposed RouterOS device; a third bug, CVE-2026-67277, allows memory disclosure or denial of service through the bandwidth-test service. CERT Polska named no victims and no sectors, noting only that MikroTik hardware is widely deployed across ISPs, data centres, enterprises and critical-infrastructure networks. That breadth is the aviation relevance rather than any confirmed airport targeting: RouterOS boxes turn up in the inexpensive, quietly-installed corners of an airport estate — remote stands and cargo sheds, car parks and shuttle depots, contractor site offices, CCTV and Wi-Fi backhaul — the places least likely to appear in an asset register and most likely to have an SSH port open for vendor support. - CERT Polska alert — reported by Industrial Cyber - Alert published 9 Sep 2026; exploitation observed since at least 2 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] CISA adds four exploited flaws on 8 September, led by a CVSS 10 pre-auth RCE in the remote-monitoring platform many airport contractors run on
item.category: Advisory — Four actively exploited flaws added to CISA KEV
item.description: The 8 September KEV batch is headed by CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, a static code-injection flaw rated CVSS 10.0 that gives unauthenticated remote code execution. N-able has confirmed exploitation in the wild, Huntress observed attacks against the platform’s API and appliance logs from 4 September, and the vendor shipped 2026.3 Hotfix 4 on 5 September — its fourth hotfix in five weeks. Federal agencies have until 11 September. Also added: two Windows zero-days confirmed exploited on the same day, CVE-2026-81963 in the Update Stack and CVE-2026-85880 in ALPC, both giving SYSTEM, plus CVE-2026-75650 in Adobe Commerce. N-central matters here because it is a managed-service platform: at airports it is the sort of console an integrator uses to reach terminal building management, access control and baggage estates. - CISA KEV catalog addition of 8 Sep 2026, with vendor confirmation from N-able, Microsoft and Adobe and telemetry reported by Huntress - Added to KEV 8 Sep 2026; N-able hotfix released 5 Sep 2026; federal deadline 11 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] September ICS Patch Tuesday: Siemens fixes an authentication bypass in protection relays, Schneider a critical flaw in Modicon M580
item.category: Advisory — September ICS Patch Tuesday
item.description: Siemens published nine advisories, seven of them on 8 September. The heaviest is SSA-142885 covering Reyrolle 7SR5 protection and control relays: fourteen CVEs in all versions before V2.70, led by CVE-2026-62645 at CVSS 9.8, where the web interface leaks enough information for an attacker to calculate current and past session identifiers and bypass authentication. Critical items also landed in Industrial Edge Management, Open Interface Services and SIMOVE Fleetmanager. Schneider Electric issued four advisories the same day, the most severe a critical authentication flaw in Modicon M580 and M580 Safety controllers, CVE-2026-3869 at CVSS 9.2, with high-severity fixes for PowerLogic T300 and EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert. Aveva patched four flaws in Pipeline Integrity Monitor, and CISA picked that one up separately on 10 September as ICSA-26-253-01: hard-coded cryptographic key CVE-2026-81821 and weak password hashing CVE-2026-81822, both CVSS 8.4, plus a missing-authorisation flaw at 5.3 and a cross-site scripting flaw at 4.7, in versions up to and including 2025 SP1 P1, fixed in the 2025 SP1 P2 security update. No exploitation has been reported for any of it. - Siemens ProductCERT advisory SSA-142885 and Schneider Electric security notifications, summarised by SecurityWeek’s ICS Patch Tuesday round-up; Aveva detail from CISA ICSA-26-253-01 as reported by ISSSource - Vendor advisories published 8 Sep 2026; CISA ICSA-26-253-01 published 10 Sep 2026 — re-verified 11 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 3 September batch covers the contractor’s VPN client and the firmware tool — IXON, Rockwell ControlFLASH, Ignition
item.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-access client, firmware tool and SCADA platform
item.description: CISA published a further set of ICS advisories on 3 September. Three are relevant to airport facility and ground OT. ICSA-26-246-02 covers the IXON VPN Client, where CVE-2026-75925 allows remote code execution with elevated privileges on the machine running the client in versions before 1.4.7 — the standard arrangement for baggage-handling, jet-bridge and de-icing vendors who support kit remotely. ICSA-26-246-03 covers Rockwell Automation ControlFLASH at V15.07 and earlier, where CVE-2026-12663 lets commands or code run at the logged-in user’s permission level; ControlFLASH is the firmware tool for the controllers under baggage systems, fuelling and airfield plant. ICSA-26-246-06 covers Inductive Automation Ignition, where any authenticated user can create projects — Ignition appears as a visualisation layer over BMS and baggage telemetry. None is reported as exploited. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-246-02 (IXON VPN Client), ICSA-26-246-03 (Rockwell Automation ControlFLASH) and ICSA-26-246-06 (Inductive Automation Ignition) - Published 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in SonicWall’s SMA1000 remote-access gateway is being exploited, and CISA gave agencies three days
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance are being exploited in the wild; the company says it found both the flaws and the exploitation internally. CVE-2026-83548, scored CVSS 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface. CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an operating-system command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console. Chained, the pair gives an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution on the appliance itself. CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2 September with a 5 September deadline for federal civilian agencies, and marked both entries as requiring forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 — a signal that patching alone does not close the incident. Affected models are the SMA1000 6210, 7210 and 8200v; SSL-VPN running on SonicWall firewalls and the SMA 100 series are not affected. - SonicWall PSIRT advisory and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition of 2 Sep 2026 — corroborated by SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer, Help Net Security and Sophos - Vendor advisory published 1 Sep 2026; added to CISA KEV 2 Sep 2026 — verified 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] A US rule now counts a cyberattack as a “not controllable” cause of delay — and ties the relief to being compliant
item.category: Regulation & Policy — US Department of Transportation
item.description: A Department of Transportation rule reported on 11 September creates a new cause-of-delay category and designates ten types of disruption as “not controllable,” cyberattacks among them. Where a carrier is compliant with the cybersecurity regulations that apply to it, it no longer owes meals, hotels or comparable amenities under its customer service plan when one of those causes grounds flights; carriers that are not compliant remain subject to the requirements. Nothing here touches an aviation control system — this is advisory-only for OT. What it changes is the cost calculus behind a grounding cyber incident, and it puts a financial edge on being able to evidence compliance, because the carrier that can show it met its obligations is the one that keeps the relief. Reporting places the rule against the backdrop of the Scattered Spider intrusions at airlines, the Collins Aerospace incident that delayed European flights and the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, and notes there is no formal accounting of how often cyberattacks previously triggered compensation claims. Carried here factually as a regulatory change, with no comment on the policy debate around it. - US Department of Transportation rule — reporting via CyberScoop - Reported 11 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] ENISA switches on the Single Reporting Platform as the Cyber Resilience Act’s vulnerability reporting duties take effect
item.category: Regulation & Policy — EU Cyber Resilience Act
item.description: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity deployed the initial operating capability of its Single Reporting Platform, announced 14 September, giving manufacturers and open-source software stewards the channel they need to meet Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations that took effect this month. Under the CRA, makers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents on a defined clock, with an early warning followed by a fuller notification. Airports and airlines are mostly beneficiaries here, but suppliers of baggage, BMS, access-control and airfield equipment placing products on the EU market now carry an active-exploitation reporting duty with a hard clock on it. Reported here factually as a regulatory milestone, without comment on the underlying policy debate. - ENISA announcement of the Single Reporting Platform initial operating capability — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Announced and reported 14 Sep 2026; CRA reporting obligations effective September 2026

item.title: [Policy] 117 federal cyber incident reporting rules across 27 agencies, and the argument that duplication costs you the first hours
item.category: Regulation — Federal cyber incident reporting
item.description: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce, drawing on GAO figures, count 117 federal cyber incident reporting regulations spread across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. Their argument is operational rather than administrative: in the first hours of an incident the same small group of people is asked to satisfy several overlapping reporting obligations on different clocks and in different formats, and that work is taken directly from response. The timing matters because CIRCIA rules are expected to be finalised this autumn. Aviation operators already sit under a dense stack — TSA security directives for regulated entities, CISA reporting, national aviation authority obligations, and separate data-protection notification duties as the Manchester case illustrated. - McCrary Institute and US Chamber of Commerce analysis citing GAO counts, reported by Industrial Cyber - Published and reported 8 Sep 2026; CIRCIA final rule expected autumn 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA and the G7 tell operators to start the post-quantum inventory now — the deadline is set by your asset lifetimes, not by them
item.category: Guidance — CISA and G7 joint call to begin the post-quantum cryptography transition; no deadline attached
item.description: CISA and the G7 Cyber Security Working Group issued a joint call on 4 September for governments and organisations to begin the transition to post-quantum cryptography, setting out a phased, risk-based approach: inventory the cryptography in use and the dependencies that carry it, identify the data and systems whose exposure would outlast the migration, and hold a written transition plan rather than a procurement wish. The statement is explicit about store-now-decrypt-later — traffic captured today can be decrypted later — and about the second-order problem, which is that authentication and firmware-signing chains rest on the same public-key algorithms. It is guidance, not a rule, and no deadline attaches. For an airport the relevance is lifecycle: BMS, access control and baggage systems specified this year will still be in service well past the migration window, and their firmware-signing and remote-access cryptography is fixed at purchase. - Joint statement from CISA and the G7 Cyber Security Working Group, reported by Industrial Cyber - Published and reported 4 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Six agencies publish outage-communication guidance for IT and OT service providers — the gap the airport disruptions exposed
item.category: Policy — Joint international guidance, incident communications
item.description: On 2 September the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security joined CISA, Australia’s ASD ACSC, NCSC-NZ, NCSC-UK and the FBI to publish joint guidance on communicating during IT and OT service outages, titled “Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers.” It calls for a written incident communications plan with defined trigger thresholds and named audiences, plain-language updates, root-cause and technical detail end users can act on, and messaging aligned with legal and regulatory duties. Aviation has the clearest recent illustration of why this is an operational control rather than a communications nicety: shared check-in and baggage platforms mean a single supplier outage propagates across independent airports simultaneously, and the airports affected are left explaining a failure they did not cause and cannot directly diagnose. - Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and CISA — joint guidance “Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers” - Published 2 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Britain moves to bar designated high-risk suppliers from critical infrastructure — without naming them publicly
item.category: Regulation & Policy — Proposed, not yet in force
item.description: The UK government has tabled late amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill that would let ministers stop critical-sector organisations from using technology suppliers designated as high risk. The Bill, introduced in November 2025 and now near the end of its passage through the Lords, already extends duties to energy, water, transport and health operators and pulls managed service providers, data centres and digital infrastructure into scope. The amendments were tabled on 24 August and reported on 2 September; they follow reporting that a small UK generating station ran manually for four days after a cyberattack. Designations would not necessarily be made public, which is the detail operators should notice: a supplier could be designated without a public list to check against, so the obligation to know your own supply chain moves from good practice to compliance exposure. None of this is in force yet, and the Bill has not completed its passage. - SecurityWeek reporting on the amendments tabled to the UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill - Amendments tabled 24 Aug 2026; reported 2 Sep 2026; not yet in force — verified 3 Sep 2026
